'''''Passiflora caerulea''''', the '''blue passionflower''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref> '''bluecrown passionflower'''<ref>{{PLANTS|id=PACA22|taxon=Passiflora caerulea|access-date=31 January 2016}}</ref> or '''common passion flower''', is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Passifloraceae]]. It is [[native plant|native]] to South America and has been introduced elsewhere.

It forms a vigorous, [[deciduous]] or semi-evergreen [[tendril]]-bearing [[vine]] growing to {{cvt|10|m|ft|0}} or more. Its leaves are palmately lobed, and its fragrant flowers are blue-white with a prominent fringe of [[Corona (perianth)|coronal]] filaments in bands of blue, white, yellow, and brown. The ovoid orange fruit grows to {{cvt|6|cm|0}} across.

The fruit is edible, but is sometimes described as having an unpalatable or unpleasant flavour. In South America, the plant is known for its medicinal properties, and is used by both the [[Toba people|Toba]] and the [[Makaa people|Maka]] peoples.

==Description==
[[File:Passiflora caerulea (makro close-up).jpg|thumbnail|''Passiflora caerulea'' flower]]''Passiflora caerulea'' is a woody vine capable of growing to {{convert|25|m|ft}} high where supporting trees are available.<ref name = "keys">{{cite web |title=Factsheet - Passiflora caerulea (Blue Passionflower) |url=https://keys.lucidcentral.org/keys/v3/eafrinet/weeds/key/weeds/Media/Html/Passiflora_caerulea_(Blue_Passionflower).htm |website=keys.lucidcentral.org |access-date=14 August 2018}}</ref> The [[leaves]] are alternate, palmately five-lobed (sometimes three, seven, or nine lobes), and are up to {{convert|10|cm|frac=4}} in length while being linear-oblong shaped.<ref name = "PIER">{{cite web |title=Passiflora caerulea: info from PIER (PIER species info) |url=http://www.hear.org/pier/species/passiflora_caerulea.htm |website=www.hear.org |publisher=Pacific Island Ecosystems at Risk project (PIER) |access-date=14 August 2018 |archive-date=28 September 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928013033/http://www.hear.org/pier/species/passiflora_caerulea.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> The base of each leaf has a flagellate-twining tendril {{convert|5-10|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} long, which twines around supporting vegetation to hold the plant up.<ref name = "keys"/>

The [[flower]] is complex, about {{convert|10|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} in diameter,<ref name = "PIER"/> with the five sepals and petals similar in appearance, whitish in colour, surmounted by a corona of blue or violet filaments, then five greenish-yellow [[stamen]]s and three purple [[stigma (botany)|stigma]]s.<ref name = "keys"/> The [[fruit]] is an oval orange-yellow [[Berry (botany)|berry]], {{convert|6|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} long by {{convert|4|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} in diameter, containing an average of 10 to 35 [[seed]]s. <ref>{{Cite web |title=CABI Digital Library |url=https://www.cabidigitallibrary.org/action/cookieAbsent |access-date=2026-05-08 |website=CABI Digital Library |language=en |doi=10.1079/cabicompendium.116172}}</ref>

While commonly used as an ornamental vine in tropical landscaping, it is an invasive, noxious weed that can take over native wildlife. Plants sometimes send underground shoots up to 15 feet from the mother plant. <ref>{{Cite web |title=PlantFiles: The Largest Plant Identification Reference Guide - Dave's Garden |url=https://davesgarden.com/guides/pf/go/1264 |access-date=2026-05-08 |website=davesgarden.com}}</ref>

=== Chemical constituents ===
Compared to ''[[Passiflora incarnata|P. incarnata]]'', this plant contains higher amounts of the [[Monoamine oxidase inhibitor|MAO-inhibitor]] [[harmine]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Frye |first1=Abigail |last2=Haustein |first2=Catherine |year=2007 |title=Extraction, Identification, and Quantification of Harmala Alkaloids in Three Species of Passiflora |journal=American Journal of Undergraduate Research |volume=6 |issue=3 |doi=10.33697/ajur.2007.020 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Etymology ==
The [[Binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] ''caerulea'' means "blue" and refers to the blue coronal filaments.<ref name="RHSLG">{{cite book |last=Harrison |first=Lorraine |title=RHS Latin for gardeners |publisher=Mitchell Beazley |year=2012 |isbn=9781845337315 |location=United Kingdom |pages=224}}</ref>

== Cultivation ==
''Passiflora caerulea'' is widely cultivated as a wall-climber or as [[groundcover]]. It is a hardy species, able to survive winter temperatures as low as {{cvt|-10|C|F|abbr=on}},<ref>{{Cite web |title=Passiflora caerulea {{!}} blue passion flower Climber Wall Shrub/RHS |url=http://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/12356/passiflora-caerulea/details |access-date=2025-09-23 |website=www.rhs.org.uk |language=en-gb}}</ref> although it requires a sheltered position facing south or west (in the Northern Hemisphere). It can become invasive, the twining shoots constantly appearing unless eradicated. It is the only ''[[Passiflora]]'' species that [[volunteer (botany)|volunteers]] in California. It has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Passiflora caerulea''|url=http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=1386|access-date=25 May 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130807063959/http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=1386|archive-date=7 August 2013|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Uses==
The fruit is edible to humans when ripe, but its flavour has been described as bland,<ref name="RHSAZ">{{cite book |title=RHS A-Z encyclopedia of garden plants |publisher=Dorling Kindersley |year=2008 |isbn=978-1405332 965 |location=United c ZKingdom |pages=1136}}</ref> undesirable<ref name="cabi">{{cite journal |last1=Popay |first1=Ian |date=2014 |title=Passiflora caerulea (blue passionflower) |url=https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/116172 |volume=CABI Compendium |doi=10.1079/cabicompendium.116172 |access-date=14 August 2018 |website=www.cabi.org|doi-access=free }}</ref> or insipid.<ref name="tetraphyllin b" /> If allowed to fully ripen in a warm climate and fall naturally from the vine, it has a mild blackberry flavour,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Passiflora caerulea (Blue Passion Flower) |url=https://www.gardenia.net/plant/passiflora-caerulea-blue-passion-flower |access-date=2025-09-23 |website=Gardenia |language=en-US}}</ref> though with a lower sugar content than commonly eaten species.{{Citation needed|date=August 2025}}[[File:Blue Passion Flower and Fruit.jpg|thumb|''P. caerulea'' flower and fruit]]
A tea can be made of the flower or leaves; but the leaves contain tetraphyllin B and epi-tetraphyllin B, [[cyanogenic glycoside]]s that liberate [[hydrogen cyanide]] when activated by enzymes. It is possible to boil away most of the cyanide.<ref name="tetraphyllin b">DS Seiglera, KC Spencera, WS Statlerb, EE Connb, JE Dunnb, '[http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0031942282851911 Tetraphyllin B and epitetraphyillin B sulphates: Novel cyanogenic glucosides from Passiflora caerulea and P. alato-caerulea] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120124073929/http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0031942282851911 |date=2012-01-24 }}', ''Phytochemistry'', 21/9 (1982), 2277-2285.</ref>

In South America, the plant is known for its medicinal uses. It is used in both [[tisane]]s (herbal tea) and dietary supplements, as well as in marmalades, ice creams, syrups and beverages.<ref name="cabi" /><ref name="mendiondo">{{cite journal |last1=Mendiondo |first1=G.M. |last2=García |first2=M.T.A. |date=2009 |title=Germination of stored and scarified seeds of ''Passiflora caerulea'' L. (Passifloraceae). |url=https://www.cabi.org/isc/abstract/20093350304 |journal=Plant Biosystems |volume=143 |issue=2 |pages=369–376 |doi=10.1080/11263500902722709 |bibcode=2009PBios.143..369M |s2cid=86722536 |issn=1126-3504 |access-date=28 August 2022 |hdl=11336/27122 |hdl-access=free |archive-date=28 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220828102308/https://www.cabi.org/isc/abstract/20093350304 |url-status=dead }}</ref> It is also used by the indigenous Argentine [[Toba people|Toba]] and [[Makaa people|Maka]] people.<ref name="cabi" /><ref name="mendiondo" />

''Passiflora caerulea'' is often used as a [[rootstock]], to which is grafted a scion of the edible [[Passiflora edulis|''P. edulis'']].<ref name="nelliekelly-passionfruit">{{cite web |title=Passionfruit |url=https://nelliekelly.com.au/passionfruit/ |website=Nellie Kelly |access-date=31 October 2023 |ref=nelliekelly-passionfruit |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231025084337/https://nelliekelly.com.au/passionfruit/ |archive-date=25 October 2023 |url-status=live}}</ref>

== In culture ==
{{See also|Passiflora#In culture}}
''Passiflora caerulea'' is the [[List of national flowers|national flower]] of [[Paraguay]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://country.paraguay.com/about_paraguay/national_flower.php |title=About Paraguay: national flower |website=Paraguay.com |access-date=23 January 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150224010526/http://country.paraguay.com/about_paraguay/national_flower.php |archive-date=24 February 2015}}</ref> Its intricate structure has generated [[Christian symbolism]], each part representing a different part of the [[Passion (Christianity)|Passion of Christ]].
